say: You give it a data set with one **outlier** in it. It tells you which summary statistics move when that value is added or removed, and which stay put.
The key idea: the mean adds up every value, so one extreme value drags it. The median only counts positions, so it barely notices.

how.higher: Higher level tests it as a short explanation on Paper 2 (2025, Q4(b), 5 marks of 30): say which statistic changes and give a reason for the mean and for the median.

example.question: Seven students recorded the minutes they spent on homework: $12, 14, 15, 17, 18, 19, 45$. The value $45$ is removed. Find how much the mean falls and how much the median falls. Which one is affected more by the outlier, and why?

steps.title: Mean and median with 45
steps.say: Add all seven values and divide by $7$. With seven values the median is the 4th one.

lines.text: The middle (4th) value is $17$, so the median is $17$.

steps.title: Mean and median without 45
steps.say: Now there are six values. Add them and divide by $6$. The median is halfway between the 3rd and 4th values.

steps.title: Compare the falls
steps.say: Subtract each new value from the old one. The mean fell by $\hl{1}{\frac{25}{6}}$ and the median fell by $\hl{2}{1}$.

steps.title: Explain why
steps.say: Say it in words. The mean uses the total, and $45$ is a big part of that total. The median only uses the middle position.

lines.text: The mean changes a lot because the outlier is added into the total. The median changes little because it depends only on the middle values, not on how large the biggest one is.

higher.tip: Give a reason for both statistics: why the mean changes and why the median does not. One half alone earns only part of the marks.

sources.quote: Two parts are required: why the mean changes

higher.tip: Use a general reason, not a single example. A particular example loses a mark.

sources.quote: Apply a * if the justification is a particular

say: You give it two distributions. It gives back a reasoned comparison of where each one is centred and how spread out it is.
The key idea: compare the **centre** (mean or median) and the **spread** (standard deviation or IQR) separately, with a number for each, then say what it means.

how.ordinary: On Ordinary Level it appears on Paper 2 (2024, Q7(a)(iii), 5 marks of 50): decide whether the spread went up or down and give a reason.

example.question: Two classes sat the same test. Five scores are taken from each. Class A: $10, 12, 13, 14, 16$. Class B: $8, 12, 14, 16, 20$. Find the mean and standard deviation of each class and compare the two classes.

steps.title: Centre of each class
steps.say: Add the scores and divide by $5$ for each class.

steps.title: Spread of Class A
steps.say: Standard deviation: square each distance from the mean, average them, then take the square root.

steps.title: Spread of Class B
steps.say: Do the same for Class B, using its mean of $14$.

steps.title: Compare
steps.say: Say which centre is higher and which spread is larger, with the numbers.

lines.text: Class B has the higher mean ($14$ against $13$), so it did slightly better on average.
Class B also has the larger standard deviation ($4$ against $2$), so its scores are more spread out. Class A is more consistent.

ordinary.tip: Always write the reason. Ticking the right box with no reason, or a wrong one, earns only partial credit.

sources.quote: Correct box ticked but no or incorrect reason given

ordinary.tip: Show your work for the mean and standard deviation. Writing the correct formula or making a real start still earns marks.

sources.quote: Work of merit, for example, effort at

say: You give it the result of one sample. It gives back a careful statement about the population, not a claim that the sample result is exactly the population value.
The key idea: a different sample would give a different result, so one sample is an **estimate**, not a fact.

example.question: A school has $1200$ students. Two different samples of $50$ students are asked if they walk to school. In the first sample $20$ walk. In the second sample $26$ walk. Find the proportion that walk in each sample. Why do the two answers differ, and what can you say about all $1200$ students?

steps.title: Proportion in each sample
steps.say: Divide the number who walk by $50$ for each sample.

steps.title: Compare the samples
steps.say: Find how far apart the two results are.

steps.title: Make a careful statement
steps.say: Each sample has different students in it, so each gives a different result. Neither one is the true value for the whole school.

lines.text: The two samples differ by $\hl{1}{0.12}$ only because different students were picked. This is **sampling variability**.
So we say: about $40\%$ to $52\%$ of the school may walk. We cannot say exactly $40\%$ or exactly $52\%$.

workedSolution.finalAnswer: 0.4 \text{ and } 0.52;\ \text{different samples give different results, so each is only an estimate}

say: You give it the sample size, $n$. It gives back the **margin of error**, how far the sample result could be from the true population value.
The key idea: a bigger sample is more reliable, so the margin shrinks as $n$ grows. The rule is $\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$.

how.higher: Higher level uses it on Paper 2 every second year (2016, 2018, 2020, 2022, 2024) as one step of a confidence interval or hypothesis test, or backwards to find $n$.
how.ordinary: Ordinary level asks for it on Paper 2 every year from 2015 to 2025, often as a 5-mark part of its own, then builds a confidence interval and tests a claim with it.

example.question: A survey asks $750$ people which radio station they prefer. Find the margin of error, as a percentage correct to one decimal place.

steps.title: Write the formula
steps.say: The margin of error depends only on the sample size $n$.

steps.title: Substitute n
steps.say: The sample has $750$ people, so put $n = 750$.

steps.title: Change to a percentage
steps.say: Multiply by $100$ and round to one decimal place.

higher.tip: Hypothesis tests are marked in four steps: hypotheses, calculation, conclusion, reason. Check you have written all four.
Write the reason using your calculation: say whether the claimed value is inside the interval or not.

sources.quote: must be based on relevant calculations

higher.tip: When you use the margin to find $n$, the scheme accepts rounding either way.

ordinary.tip: Round the answer and say so. A mark is lost if the percentage is not rounded or is rounded wrongly.

sources.quote: Apply a * for no or incorrect rounding

ordinary.tip: Write the formula $\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$ first. A correct formula alone earns partial credit.
The margin is a percentage, so multiply by $100$. Leaving it as a decimal only earns partial credit.
Give a conclusion and a reason when you test a claim: whether the value is inside the interval or outside it.
